title: Sum of the Roman doctrine: a middle cult between divine majesty and merely civil honor
source_text: I. Thesibus superioribus, quam breviter & dilucide a nobis fieri potuit, exposuimus doctrinam Ecclesiae & Scholae Romanae, circa Angelorum & hominum Sanctorum cultum & venerationem. Eorum autem quae paulo fusius a nobis dicta sunt haec summa est. Ecclesiam Romanam Angelis & hominibus Sanctis cultum aliquem deferre, qui medius est inter eum quem Dei Majestas exigit, & eum qui debetur illis, qui inter homines caeteros eminent, vel dignitate ac potestate civili, vel donis, virtute, ac praestantia quadam, quae tamen ordinem naturae non excedunt.
pass_a_gloss: In the theses above, as briefly and clearly as could be done, the doctrine of the Roman Church and School about the cult and veneration of angels and holy men was set out. The sum of what was said a little more fully is this: the Roman Church pays holy angels and holy men a cult that stands in the middle, between the cult which the majesty of God requires and the cult owed to other men who stand out by civil dignity and power, or by gifts, virtue, and a certain excellence that still does not go beyond the order of nature.
pass_b_english: Le Blanc opens Pars Secunda by compressing the Roman account he has already given.
Rome, on that account, assigns angels and canonized people a middle honor.
That honor sits above civic respect for outstanding neighbors and below the worship God's majesty requires.
The lower comparison is with rank, power, and natural gifts, not with anything beyond nature.

choices.why: Marks the civil comparison as still natural, not supernatural glory.
